verdicts.trueWording: The “where” is the opening scene, and the “why”…
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200, browser UA). Quote is word-for-word in the section 'You May Ask Yourself, How Did I Get Here?', which first poses the two reader questions (where am I / why am I here) that the claim maps onto scene and hook. Byline Shawn Merwin, D&D Beyond, Oct 23 2019, all confirmed on page.

Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). Quote verbatim in the final substantive paragraph of the Peterson excerpt; the same sentence ties Keep on the Borderlands (B2), shipped with the Moldvay Basic Set, to the height of the D&D boom in 1981. Page is introduced as a never-before-seen piece cut from Peterson's Game Wizards, so the attribution to Peterson holds.

Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). Quote verbatim in the Introduction under the heading 'The Base Rules', in a sentence about the GAZ books being designed for beginning players; the antecedent 'these books' is the Gazetteer line, so the claim's scope is right.

verdicts.trueWording: “descriptions in this chapter are mostly meant for players”
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). Quote verbatim, but it sits in the section 'Gaz 1 Part 2: Maps, Characters and More History of Karameikos', NOT 'Gaz 1 Part 4: The Lay of the Land' as the citation's page field says - same URL, wrong section; fix the locator before reuse. The claim's 'rather than the DM' is the contrast implied by 'mostly meant for players', not words on the page; the stated purpose there is letting players decide where their characters are from.

verdicts.trueWording: “Unlike Gygax, whose prose resembled a baroque sermon”
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). Quote verbatim inside the section 'The Teacher: Frank Mentzer and the Human Face of D&D', where Gygax's prose is the foil for Mentzer's teacherly style. Byline Serban Ionita, The RPG Gazette, posted November 11 2025.

verdicts.trueWording: “Literary and media scholars studied the forms of textuality, authorship”
verdicts.note: PDF fetched (HTTP 200) and text-extracted with pypdf, 31 pages. Quote verbatim; the sentence names literary and media scholars, and it sits inside the paragraph that opens 'In the 2000s, scholars in fields such as sociology...', so the decade limb is carried by the paragraph frame. This is the White Rose accepted manuscript of the Routledge chapter.

Same PDF, same page-region as index 817. Quote verbatim. Two nuances worth carrying: the chapter says 'like' Peterson and Appelcline, marking them as exemplars rather than the only producers, and its object is 'TRPGs and RPGs more generally', slightly wider than the claim's 'tabletop role-playing games'.

verdicts.trueWording: “the most important thing to know about world building is, who”
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). Quote verbatim, twice on the page (body line and pull-quote), spoken by Wolfgang Baur in the opening exchange after the host's first prompt. The claim drops Baur's hedge 'I think'; the sentence completes by asking who you are doing it for, which is the claim's second limb. Seminar part 1, dated July 14 2025.

verdicts.trueWording: “this town hates this town over here”
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). Quote verbatim, spoken by Zeb Cook in the exchange on conflict, about the worst worldbuilding books being 'literally just lists of places and people'. The claim's 'never saying' renders the page's 'They don't spend any time saying', and 'the town next to it' renders 'this town over here'.

verdicts.trueWording: “You are not creating a world for yourself”
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). Quote verbatim, Cook speaking, prefaced by 'if I'm doing something for publication', which supports the claim's 'published'; the next sentence supplies the 'for other players to take and use' limb. The citation's page field says 'exchange on choosing a theme'; the actual context is the exchange on deciding what to work on and for whom.

verdicts.trueWording: “needs to be super clear what kind of adventures take place”
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). Quote verbatim, twice (body and pull-quote), spoken by Richard Green. The claim's 'at once' renders the page's condition 'when you pick up a new game or a new setting book'; the sentence continues with what the characters are going to get up to.

verdicts.trueWording: “to stack as many boxes of dynamite as possible”
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). The Gnome Stew review quotes Baur directly - 'As Wolfgang Baur says in his opening essay' - and closes the quotation with the page cite '(12)', so both the opening-essay limb and the p.12 locator are on the page. Note this is the reviewer quoting the book, not the book itself; the primary source is Kobold Guide to Worldbuilding p.12.

verdicts.trueWording: “conceptualizing TRPGs as, first and foremost, “literary gametexts””
verdicts.note: PDF fetched (HTTP 200) and text-extracted with pypdf, 12 pages, International Journal of Role-Playing issue 18. Quote verbatim in section '1. INTRODUCTION', where Mizer attributes the framing to Carbonell (2019, 3) alongside Gagne and contrasts it with his own anthropological angle.

verdicts.trueWording: “emerges as a set of practices which are only later codified”
verdicts.note: Same PDF, section '1. INTRODUCTION', two sentences after the index-839 quote. Quote verbatim; the page reads 'I will argue the role-playing game emerges as...', so it is Mizer's own argument, and the codification is 'in the formulation of a gametext', matching the claim's final limb.

verdicts.trueWording: “centering the gametexts and gametools that create gameplay”
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). Quote verbatim; the page's own frame is that Dread Trident 'claims to add to posthuman theorization' by this approach, i.e. the reviewer reporting the book's claim. Burton endorses the substance elsewhere in the review (the book expands posthuman discourse, shifting posthumanism from bodies to spaces), so the claim's 'theorises the posthuman by centering...' holds. Byline Adrianna Burton, Analog Game Studies, January 9 2022.
